title: Keep a writer's buffer from holding on to a replay

blocks.text: Each writer thread of the audit service collects records in a `RecordBuffer` and drains it to storage in batches of a few thousand. After an outage, a replay pushes hundreds of thousands of records through the same buffers. A week after the last outage, a heap dump shows every writer's buffer still holding an array of hundreds of thousands of slots, all of them empty. Decoding a frame, whose header gives its row count before the rows arrive one by one, also shows the buffer's array being copied while the rows go in.

items: `prepareFor(incoming)`: called before a frame's rows are added;
`drain()`: hands back the records added since the last drain, in order, and leaves the buffer empty.

blocks.text: When you're done, a buffer drained after a replay keeps no more than `NORMAL_BATCH` slots, a normal batch neither reallocates the array nor grows it again, and a frame's rows go in without the array growing while they are added. About seven lines in total.
The tests read the buffer's array by reflection.

cases.says: a drain hands back single records and frame rows in the order they were added, and leaves the buffer empty
a replay of tens of thousands of records is drained whole and in order
after a replay is drained the buffer keeps no more slots than a normal batch needs, and the next normal batch doesn't grow it
draining a normal batch keeps the buffer's array, and the next normal batch goes into the same array
a frame added to a buffer that already holds records grows the array, if at all, before its first row, never while its rows go in

origin.section: An ArrayList Grows by Half When Full, and Nothing Shrinks on Its Own

concepts: An ArrayList grows by half when full and keeps its array through clear(); trimToSize() leaves zero slots, and ensureCapacity takes the total the list must hold.
